title: RBI Purpose Code for Receiving International Payments
summary: Find the RBI purpose codes for inward remittances, learn how to choose the right code, and understand their role in receiving international payments.
body_markdown:
## Purpose code list for inward remittance (by category)


Here is the list of purpose codes you are most likely to use (based on the most searched purpose code on Google), grouped by the kind of international payment you are receiving. This is not the complete RBI schedule (which runs into dozens more codes for things like shipping, insurance, and government transactions), but it covers what freelancers, exporters, and service businesses deal with most often.

## How to pick the correct purpose code (step-by-step)


1.


**Identify what the money is actually for.** Not your industry, not your company type, but the specific work this particular invoice covers.


2.


**Check if it is goods or a service.** Goods exports fall under the P01 series. Services fall under P08, P09, or P10 depending on the type of service.


3.


**Match the code to the exact nature of the service.** A software build is P0802. A consulting or BPO engagement is P1006. A market research project is P1007. These get mixed up often, so read your own invoice line item carefully before picking a code.


4.


**Check if it is a full payment or an advance.** For goods, a shipped-order payment is P0102, while an advance is P0103.


5.


**Keep it consistent with any related filing.** If you are filing SOFTEX for software exports or EDPMS for goods exports, the purpose code needs to match that filing. If this is unmatched, then your export record can be flagged as unrealised.


If you are ever unsure, it is always better to have someone double-check before the payment is initiated rather than after. This is one of the things[Infinity’s](https://www.infinityapp.in/) personal account managers help with directly; they will confirm the right code with you before your client sends the payment, so you are not troubleshooting it after the money is already stuck.


## What your client or payer should write in the wire transfer


The purpose code your bank applies is often influenced by what your overseas client writes in the payment narration. A vague description like “consulting fee” or “services” on a software payment can push your bank towards the wrong code, even if your invoice is perfectly clear.


Before your client sends a payment, share the exact nature of the work with them in plain language (for example, “payment for software development services”) so their bank’s narration and your invoice describe the same thing. This one step prevents a large share of purpose code mismatches before they even happen.


## What happens if you use the wrong purpose code


Using an incorrect purpose code does not always block a payment outright, but it usually creates one or more of these problems:


-


**Delayed or held credit.** Your bank may pause crediting the amount to your account until the code is confirmed or corrected.


-


**Mismatched export records.** If you are filing[SOFTEX](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/softex-for-indian-exporters) or EDPMS, a mismatched code can leave your export shipment or invoice showing as unrealised.


-


**FIRA/FIRC discrepancies.** The purpose code appears on your Foreign Inward Remittance Advice or Certificate, so a wrong code here can cause issues later if you need it for GST refund claims or tax filing.


-


**Repeated scrutiny.** Banks tend to flag accounts that repeatedly use incorrect codes, which can mean more questions on future remittances.


## How to fix a wrong purpose code


If you notice the wrong code has already been applied to a payment, here is what to do:


1.


**Contact your bank’s forex or remittance desk immediately.** The sooner you raise it, the easier the correction.


2.


**Share the transaction details.** This includes the UTR (Unique Transaction Reference) number, amount, currency, and the date the payment was credited.


3.


**Submit supporting documents.** An invoice, contract, or work order that clearly states the actual nature of the payment is usually enough.


4.


**Request a corrected FIRA or FIRC.** Once the bank updates the code, ask for a revised document reflecting the correct purpose, since this is what you will need for any future compliance or refund filing.


This is another place where having support matters. Infinity auto-generates your FIRA for every payment you receive. If ever a correction is needed, your dedicated account manager will help you directly rather than leaving you to chase the bank’s forex desk on your own.


## FAQs


### What is a purpose code for inward remittance?


It is a 5-character RBI code, starting with P, that tells your bank why a foreign payment has arrived in your account. It is mandatory under FEMA reporting.


### What is the difference between P codes and S codes?


P codes are used for inward remittances (money coming into India). S codes are used for outward remittances (money going out of India).


### Which purpose code should freelancers use?


It depends on the nature of the work. Software and IT freelancers typically use P0802. Consultants, including BPO and KPO work, typically use P1006. Design, research, or advertising-related work usually falls under P1007.


### What happens if the purpose code is wrong?


Your payment may be delayed or held by the bank, and your export or FIRA records can show a mismatch. You can request a correction from your bank with supporting documents.


### Where do I find my purpose code after receiving a payment?


It is listed on your FIRA or FIRC, usually alongside the transaction’s UTR number and payment details.


### Can I correct a purpose code after the transaction is reported?


Yes, in most cases. Contact your bank with the correct details and supporting documents such as an invoice. The process varies slightly by bank, so it is best to raise it as soon as you notice the error.


### Do domestic transfers like UPI or RTGS need a purpose code?


No. Purpose codes apply only to foreign inward and outward remittances reported under FEMA, not domestic transfers.
